title: A gasifier is a ledger: balance the atoms, minimise the Gibbs energy, size the walls
summary: Gasification can be reasoned about with three tools: atom and energy balances that say what must add up, an equilibrium calculation that says where the chemistry wants to go, and heat-transfer resistances that say how big and how hot the hardware must be.

media.alt: Stacked bar chart of five cases A to E. Each bar is split into a teal part 1 at the bottom and an amber part 2 on top; a red dashed line with dots marks the total of each bar.
media.caption: Reference render of plot class F12.4 (stacked ledger) with synthetic demonstration data, not a rig result.

source.note: Standard chemical thermodynamics and heat transfer at textbook level. The equilibrium numbers were computed here with Cantera 3.1 using the GRI-Mech 3.0 thermodynamic data for the gas phase only (no char, no tar). The figure is the design system's synthetic F12.4 render.

read_the_figure.question: Where does the total come from, and does the ledger close?
read_the_figure.axes: x: the cases being compared (here A to E; for a rig, runs or operating points). y: the quantity being accounted for, in one unit. Each bar stacks its contributions, so the top of the stack is the total.
look_at: The total line against the top of each stack: they must coincide. If they do not, something is missing from the ledger.
The lower segment is the easiest to compare across cases because it starts at zero; the upper segment is easier to read as a share of its own bar.
Which contribution drives the difference between the highest and the lowest bar.
The unit and basis on the axis: kilograms or megajoules, per kilogram of fuel or per hour.
read_the_figure.proves: Parts that sum to the total within the stated uncertainty show the balance is complete, so the shares you read off are meaningful.
if_wrong: A gap between the stack and the total: an unmeasured stream, a leak, or a unit mismatch.
A loss term that is negative: a sign error or a mislabelled inlet.
Shares computed from bars of different bases: percentages of different totals cannot be compared.
must_check: Every inlet and outlet stream is present, including losses to the surroundings.
One basis for all bars (per kg of dry fuel, for instance).
Uncertainty on each segment, or at least on the closure error.
Lower or higher heating value stated.

terms.meaning: Air actually fed divided by the air needed for complete combustion of the fuel. A gasifier runs well below 1, so there is not enough oxygen to burn everything.
Mass of steam fed per mass of dry fuel. It adds hydrogen and oxygen without adding nitrogen.
The product gas, mainly H2, CO, CO2, CH4, H2O and N2 when air is used.
The heat released by burning a fuel with the product water left as vapour, per kilogram of fuel.
The atoms of each element entering equal the atoms leaving, whatever molecules they sit in.
The function that a mixture at fixed temperature and pressure minimises at equilibrium.
The change of Gibbs energy when one mole of species i is added. At equilibrium it follows from the element constraints.
A number, function of temperature only, that fixes the ratio of products to reactants at equilibrium.
A system at equilibrium that is disturbed shifts to partly undo the disturbance.
Temperature difference divided by heat flow. Resistances in series add, like electrical ones.
The average driving temperature difference of a heat exchanger whose two ends differ.
A flow diagram whose band widths are proportional to the amount carried, so conservation shows up as widths adding up.

remember: ER = (air fed) / (air for complete combustion). Gasification: well below 1.
Atoms are conserved, molecules are not. One balance per element.
Equilibrium at fixed T and P: minimise G subject to the element balances.
For any atom-conserving reaction, sum of nu_i mu_i = 0 gives the product of (activity)^nu = K(T).
d ln K / dT = Delta H / (R T^2): endothermic reactions gain with temperature, exothermic lose.
Series resistances add. Plane wall: L / (k A). Tube wall: ln(r_o / r_i) / (2 pi k L).
Energy in = energy out + losses. A Sankey diagram draws it.

understand.title: Balances say what is possible, equilibrium says what is likely
understand.text: Atom balances leave two free numbers when the gas has five species. Something must pick them. Equilibrium thermodynamics picks the composition with the lowest Gibbs energy. Real reactors do not reach it, but it is the reference the real composition is measured against.

understand.title: Why steam helps hydrogen
understand.text: Steam supplies hydrogen atoms and, by the water-gas shift, converts CO into more H2. The shift is exothermic, so it is favoured at low temperature, while methane destruction is favoured at high temperature. The operating temperature is therefore a compromise, not a maximum.

understand.title: Why a Sankey diagram
understand.text: A balance is only useful when it closes. Drawing each stream as a band whose width is its share of the input makes a missing or double-counted stream visible at once.

steps.title: Stoichiometric air and the equivalence ratio
steps.note: Write the fuel per mole of carbon. Oxygen atoms on the right are 2 + x/2, on the left y + 2a, which gives a (verified symbolically). For CH1.4O0.6 a = 1.05 mol O2, or 5.0 mol air, per mole of carbon.

steps.title: Element balances: three equations, five unknowns
steps.tex: \mathbf A\,\mathbf n=\mathbf b,\qquad \mathbf A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0&0&1\\0&0&2&2&4\\1&2&0&1&0\end{pmatrix}\ \text{(rows C, H, O; columns CO, CO}_2,\mathrm H_2,\mathrm H_2\mathrm O,\mathrm{CH}_4)
steps.note: The matrix has rank 3, so its null space has dimension 2: two independent reactions (for instance the water-gas shift and methane reforming) are undetermined by balances alone. Verified: A times each reaction vector is zero.

steps.title: Energy balance and the cold gas efficiency
steps.note: The first law for the steady reactor, with enthalpies including the heat of formation. The cold gas efficiency is the share of the fuel's heating value that leaves as chemical energy in the gas. The rest is sensible heat, char, tar and losses: the bands of a Sankey diagram.

steps.title: Equilibrium as a constrained minimum
steps.note: At fixed T and P a closed mixture minimises G. The logarithm is the ideal-gas mixing term, y_i the mole fraction. The constraints are exactly the element balances above.

steps.title: The constraint gives the equilibrium constant
steps.note: Lagrange multipliers lambda_k attach to the element constraints. Any reaction that conserves atoms has a vector nu with A nu = 0, so the weighted sum of chemical potentials vanishes and the mass-action law follows. Verified: this is the null-space statement of step 2.

steps.title: Temperature: van't Hoff
steps.tex: \frac{d\ln K}{dT}=\frac{\Delta H^\circ}{RT^2},\qquad \mathrm{CO}+\mathrm H_2\mathrm O\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{CO}_2+\mathrm H_2,\ \Delta H^\circ<0
steps.note: Verified symbolically for K = exp(-dH/RT) at constant dH. For the water-gas shift, computed from the GRI-Mech thermodynamic data, K falls from 28.3 at 600 K to 1.44 at 1000 K and 0.73 at 1200 K. Hot favours CO, cold favours H2: Le Chatelier.

steps.title: Steam and pressure
steps.tex: Q=\frac{y_{\mathrm{CO}_2}y_{\mathrm H_2}}{y_\mathrm{CO}y_{\mathrm H_2\mathrm O}}<K\ \text{on adding steam}\Rightarrow\text{shift right};\qquad K_y=K\left(\frac{P^\circ}{P}\right)^{\Delta\nu}
steps.note: Adding H2O lowers the reaction quotient below K, so the shift runs right and makes H2. The shift has no mole change so pressure does not move it, but methane reforming has delta-nu = +2, so high pressure keeps CH4 in. Computed gas-only equilibria at 900 K and 1 atm give H2/CO = 0.91, 1.80, 3.24 for 0.4, 0.8, 1.5 mol steam per mol C; methane is 0.091 at 1 atm and 0.237 at 10 atm (0.8 mol H2O per mol C).

steps.title: Heat through a tube wall
steps.note: Steady conduction without a source in a cylinder; the two boundary temperatures fix C1 and C2 (verified with sympy). The convective layers are R = 1/(h A). All resistances sit in series, so the largest one controls the heat flow.

steps.title: Sizing the tube length
steps.tex: Q=\dot m\,c_p\,(T_\mathrm{out}-T_\mathrm{in})=U\,\pi D L\,\Delta T_\mathrm{lm},\quad \Delta T_\mathrm{lm}=\frac{\Delta T_1-\Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1/\Delta T_2)}
steps.note: The duty fixes the length once the overall coefficient U is known. For 0.02 kg/s of gas with c_p = 1.1 kJ/(kg K) heated from 300 to 600 K inside a wall held at 800 C, with U = 100 W/(m^2 K) and D = 50 mm: Q = 6.6 kW, the log-mean difference is 611 K and L = 0.69 m. Check the wall temperature limit before trusting the length.

worked.title: How much heat does an insulated reactor tube lose, and how hot is its skin?
worked.problem: A tube with inner radius 25 mm and outer radius 30 mm is steel (k = 16 W/(m K)), wrapped in insulation (k = 0.1 W/(m K)) to a radius of 80 mm. Gas at 800 C flows inside (h_i = 100 W/(m^2 K)), the room is at 25 C (h_o = 10 W/(m^2 K)). Find the heat loss per metre and the outer surface temperature.

solution.text: The four resistances per metre of tube, in K m/W.
Add them and divide the temperature difference.
The outer skin is one resistance away from the room.

worked.answer: About 425 W per metre of tube, with the outer surface at 109 C. The insulation carries 86 percent of the total resistance and the steel about 0.1 percent, so the steel thickness hardly matters and the insulation thickness decides the loss. A skin at 109 C is a burn hazard: it needs more insulation or a guard.

analyze.q: Double the insulation conductivity from 0.1 to 0.2 W/(m K). By roughly how much does the heat loss change, and which resistance is now the second largest?
analyze.hint: The insulation term is 1.56 of 1.83 K m/W.

analyze.q: The gasifier is run hotter at the same steam rate. Which products rise and which fall in an equilibrium calculation, and why does the hydrogen yield not rise without limit?
analyze.hint: One reaction is endothermic and one is exothermic.

analyze.q: A mass balance closes to 94 percent. List three places the missing 6 percent could be, and how each would show up on the Sankey diagram.
analyze.hint: Tar, char and fines, sampling losses, unmeasured flow.

evaluate.q: Equilibrium predicts more hydrogen than a real gasifier delivers. Is the equilibrium model then useless, or useful for something specific?
evaluate.hint: Upper bound, trend with T and S/B, benchmark for kinetic models.

evaluate.q: An energy balance on a rig closes within 3 percent using thermocouples whose error is 5 K. What would make you doubt the closure anyway?
evaluate.hint: Compensating errors and the heating-value basis.

create: Draw the Sankey diagram you would measure on a small rig: the streams in, the streams out, which one you can measure directly and which you obtain by difference.
Write a ten-line equilibrium solver for CO, CO2, H2, H2O and CH4 from given element totals using the two reaction constants, and check it against a Gibbs-minimising library at three temperatures.

checks.q: Why does 'minimise G subject to element balances' lead to the mass-action law?
checks.hint: What is sum of nu_i times a_ki for a reaction that conserves atoms?
checks.answer: At the minimum each chemical potential is a combination of the element multipliers, mu_i = sum_k lambda_k a_ki. A reaction that conserves atoms has sum_i a_ki nu_i = 0 for every element, so sum_i nu_i mu_i = 0. Writing mu_i with its logarithm gives the product of activities equal to exp(-delta g0/RT).

checks.q: One mole of CO and one of steam reach shift equilibrium at 1000 K, where K = 1.435. What fraction of the CO is converted? Ignore other reactions.
checks.hint: K = xi^2/(1 - xi)^2, since the mole count does not change.
checks.answer: Take the square root: xi/(1 - xi) = sqrt(1.435) = 1.198, so xi = 1.198/2.198 = 0.545. About 54.5 percent converts at 1000 K; at 600 K (K = 28.3) the conversion would be 84 percent.

checks.q: Raising pressure from 1 to 10 atm raised the equilibrium methane fraction from 0.09 to 0.24. Why, and what would you do to the pressure if you want a hydrogen-rich gas?
checks.hint: Count moles in CH4 + H2O -> CO + 3 H2.
checks.answer: Reforming turns 2 mol into 4, so higher pressure pushes the equilibrium back toward methane (Le Chatelier). For hydrogen you run at low pressure and high temperature, or accept the methane and use it as fuel, at the cost of compressing the product downstream.

checks.q: Two groups compare cold gas efficiency, one using LHV and the other HHV. How far apart can they be, and what must be stated?
checks.hint: Water in the products and in the fuel moisture.
checks.answer: The heating-value basis changes both numerator and denominator by different amounts because the gas and the fuel have different hydrogen contents and water, so the efficiencies can differ by several percentage points. State LHV or HHV, wet or dry fuel, and whether sensible heat is counted.

checks.q: You need the outer skin below 60 C at the same gas temperature. How would you size the insulation, and what would you check afterwards?
checks.hint: Skin temperature is T_amb + q' R_o, and q' depends on the insulation radius.
checks.answer: Solve T_s = 60 C for the outer radius with the series-resistance formula (increase r_2 until it holds, noting R_o falls and R_ins rises). Afterwards check the insulation's maximum service temperature at its inner face (about 772 C here), the weight and the heat loss in watts, which sets the heater power.
